  and the end-of-turn event to a script that appends to the log. The end-of-turn hook
  receives a path to the session transcript on stdin.
- **Cursor / Windsurf** — a project rules file, plus whatever export or history
  mechanism the app provides. Check whether the app writes a session store on disk you
  can read from.
- **Codex CLI / Aider / other** — check for a session log, a transcript flag, or a
  config hook. Most write a session file somewhere; find it and extract from it.

checked, and wrap the session instead. Saying "my tool cannot do this" without having
checked is the wrong answer.

your repo, publicly, so treat them as part of the submission.

diffs, or the retries the model made on its own. Just: what you asked, and what came
back at the end of that turn.

- The prompt, verbatim and in full. No truncation, no paraphrase, no cleanup.
- The final response for that prompt, in full, including the ones where it got it wrong.

- The model name, so a switch mid-build is visible.

- **Interrupted replies** (when you stopped me mid-answer) weren't logged. They're now recovered and marked "interrupted".
- **Your answers to my multiple-choice questions** weren't logged. They are now.
- **Messages the tool sends itself** (background task notices, my helper agents' reports, the "usage limit reset" message) were logged as if you'd typed them. They're now labelled as system messages.
- **The history from before logging existed** (the research phase and early build) was rebuilt into a separate file clearly marked "backfilled".
- **Logging is fully raw now**, as you chose.
- **Both canary tests are real now**: one typed by you in this session, one from a separate session. The earlier ones were simulated. The separate-session test caught three bugs itself, all fixed and left visible in the log.
- **`CAPTURE-TEST.md` was rewritten**, including owning my wrong call that the 8x page was suspicious.

## 2. The redesign: it's now "Cue"

- **Meeting page:** opens on a "who spoke when" map, with a lane per speaker and their share of the talking. Highlights and action items are pinned where they happened, and clicking anywhere jumps there.
- **Beside the map:**
  - summary (General or Sales)
  - action items that jump to where they were agreed
  - highlights with notes
  - a transcript that follows playback and can be searched
- **Player:** its own controls, with skip ±15s, 1×–2× speed, and keyboard shortcuts (space, arrows, H to highlight).
- **Other pages redone:** landing page, meetings list (each with a mini timeline), search that lists every matching moment, drag-and-drop upload, and the shared-link page.
- **Look:** warm off-white "paper", a serif for headings, one orange accent, and a new logo.
- **Removed:** the fake "Team Calls" page.

## 3. Behind the scenes

- **"Try the demo" button:** reviewers get in without signing in, with their own copy of the samples. Demo accounts clean themselves up after 3 days.
- **Every new account gets the samples.** Before, only the first person to ever sign in did, and everyone else saw an empty list.
- **Action items remember when they were said,** so they can sit on the timeline.
- **Fixed a security hole:** AI-written summary text could inject code into the public share page.

## 4. Sample data, deployment and cleanup

- **A new 8-person, 8.5-minute sample meeting** ("Q4 Planning"), made with synthesized voices, since that's the case the design is built for.
- **All sample audio converted from WAV to MP3** (36.5 MB down to 5 MB), so it loads fast.
- **README rewritten** to explain Cue and the design choices.
- **Deployed** to the same live URL.
- **Your account reset** to four fresh samples. Your old uploads and my test accounts are deleted.

content:
Yes, this can be done without any paid service.

**Why it happens:** Whisper, the free transcription model we use (running on Groq's free tier), only produces words and timestamps. It has no idea who is talking, so every upload comes out as one "Speaker". The samples look right only because their speaker timing was created along with the audio.

**Two free ways to tell voices apart:**

1. **Listen to the voices (recommended).** An open-source library, sherpa-onnx, figures out who spoke when from the sound itself. I just checked: its Node package (v1.13.8) supports this and has a 33 MB Linux build. With two small open models (about 6 MB and 30 MB), it would run inside our existing upload step on Vercel, with no outside service. It's accurate at telling voices apart, but gives "Speaker 1, 2, 3" rather than names.
   - **Tradeoffs:** it adds about 70 MB to the server code, uploads would take longer (my rough guess is 30–90 seconds more for a 15-minute call, not measured yet), and I need to confirm it fits Vercel's limits.
2. **Read the conversation.** Ask the AI model we already use to split the transcript into speakers from cues like turn-taking and questions and answers. Quick to build, and fine for 2–3 people talking back and forth. It's unreliable for bigger meetings, because it can't hear anything.

**Getting real names (works with either):**
- **Name detection:** the AI reads the transcript for things like "Thanks, Priya" or people introducing themselves, and suggests a name for each speaker.
- **Rename in the app:** click "Speaker 2", type "Priya", and it updates the whole meeting. You could also merge two speakers if one person got split. This is the fallback that always works.

**My suggestion:** option 1 plus both name methods. I'd start with a short test: run it on our sample meetings, where we know exactly who spoke when, so we get a real accuracy score, and check it fits Vercel. If it doesn't fit, I'd fall back to option 2 with the same naming features.

Want me to start that test?
